title: Biomimetic actuator crafted from a relaxor ferroelectric polymer nanocomposite

paper_content.abstract: Soft actuators have garnered widespread attention due to their distributed actuation and higher rortolerance. However, fabricating biomimetic actuators with small-size, simple structure, low energy consumption, and multi-functionality remains challenging. Here, we present a monolayer nanocomposite achieved by incorporating polymer dots into a polyvinylidene fluoride terpolymer. Through interfacial hydrogen bonding and temperature modulation, a gradient distribution of highly polarized regions is achieved within the nanocomposite. This yields ultra high electromechanical performance, with an actuation strain of 14.4% and an output mechanical energy density of 1.92 J cm−³ at 100 MV m−¹. Multifunctional soft actuators are formed from this nanocomposite, weighing only 50 mg, and can skillfully imitate both caterpillar crawling and butterfly flight, unlocking the potential for multimodal locomotion. This insect-sized bionic actuator consumes a mere 3-8 mW. The combination of simple architecture and low energy consumption may pave the way for future development of truly bionic soft robots.

paper_content.results:
Fabrication and interaction mechanism
Fig. 1a shows a schematic of the fabrication process for the relaxor ferroelectric polymer nanocomposite with a gradient distribution of all-trans conformations, which consists of relaxor ferroelectric P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) terpolymers and polymer dots (PDs) (See Method section for details). Briefly, PDs were initially prepared by hydrothermal cross-linking with citric acid and ethylenediamine following the classical bottom-up approach24. And PDs were homogeneously mixed with pre-dissolved PVDF terpolymer solution by tip ultrasonic. After that, the solution was drop-casted onto a clean glass and followed by a progressive heating process (60–120 °C) to evaporate the solvent. When the temperature exceeds 60 °C, there is a significant difference in solvent evaporation rates between the upper (in contact with air) and the lower (in contact with a glass substrate) surfaces of the composite film, which results in a higher proportion of all-trans conformations in the lower layer compared to the upper layer25. Note that this optimized composite film is defined as terpolymer/PDs-G, and the pure terpolymer film prepared using a progressive heating process is defined as terpolymer-G. After peeling off the film from the glass substrate, carbon nanotubes (CNTs) dispersion was spray-coated on two surfaces of the polymer film to achieve the elliptically shaped active area as an electrode. By utilizing the abundant functional groups on the PD surface to form hydrogen bonds with the fluorine atoms in the polymer chains, the proportion of all-trans conformations in the composite film is increased (Fig. 1b), resulting in the construction of films with a gradient distribution of all-trans conformations (Fig. 1c). The nanocomposite terpolymer/PDs-G film prepared using this strategy exhibits a giant strain in the presence of an electrical field (Fig. 1d). Under an applied electric field of 42 MV m−1, the terpolymer/PDs-G film folds together directly, while the terpolymer-G film undergoes only minor deformation (Supplementary Movie 1).

Fig. 1e and Supplementary Fig. S1a illustrate the thickness strain (S 3) of nanocomposites with different concentrations of PDs as a function of electric field. As PD content increases, the strain initially rises and then decreases, and the composite with 0.5 wt% PDs content has the highest strain. This is due to the best hydrogen bonding interactions between PDs and the terpolymer in the 0.5 wt% PDs doped composites. To assess the robustness and standardization potential of our gradual-heating process, we rigorously evaluated its batch-to-batch reproducibility. Multiple independent batches of the terpolymer/PDs-G (c = 0.5 wt%) composite were fabricated under identical conditions. The electrostrictive strain values of these new batches were highly consistent with the data from our original batch reported above (Supplementary Fig. S2). The exceptionally low standard deviations relative to the mean values confirm that our fabrication process is stable, straightforward to standardize, and yields highly reproducible, high-performance materials. To analyze the reason for the superior performance of the gradient-distributed structure composite, we investigated the effect of PDs introduction and the impact of the gradient structure on the performance of the nanocomposites using the control variable approach, respectively. First, to study the influence of PDs on the composite from a microscopic perspective, we prepared uniformly distributed composite films (named as terpolymer/PDs) and terpolymer films by the slow solvent evaporation method at a constant temperature of 60 °C. The Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectrum of PDs (Fig. 1f) confirms the presence of amide functional groups, as evidenced by their vibrational fingerprints centered at 1562 cm−1 (N-H in-plane bending), 1704 cm−1 (C=O stretching of the amide bond), and 3300 cm−1 (N-H stretching). As shown in Fig. 1g, after incorporating PDs into the terpolymer, the bending absorption peak of the N-H (in-plane bending) shifted to 1550 cm−1, and a very obvious absorption peak appeared at 1636 cm−1 which increased with the increase of PDs content. This phenomenon is attributed to the formation of hydrogen bonds between the N-H of the amide bond in the PDs and the fluorine atom in the terpolymers26, and hydrogen bonds can induce the formation of all-trans conformation in PVDF-based polymers27. The gradient distribution of the all-trans conformation, rather than the spatial distribution of PDs, is the primary outcome of our gradual-heating process. While the PDs are uniformly dispersed due to good compatibility with the terpolymer matrix, the thermal gradient during film formation creates a corresponding solvent evaporation rate gradient. The bottom surface of the film, experiencing a slower evaporation rate, facilitates a more orderly arrangement of polymer chains into the all-trans conformation. The PDs, rich in hydrogen-bonding sites, locally amplify this effect by stabilizing the all-trans conformation around them. Thus, the driving force is the evaporation rate gradient templated by the thermal gradient, which directly programs the gradient in polymer chain conformation.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern shows the (110/200) reflection of composites shifting towards higher angles (Fig. 2a). This indicates that the introduction of PDs reduced the interchain spacing of the terpolymer. By comparing FT-IR spectra, we observed an increase in the all-trans conformation within the terpolymer following the introduction of PDs (Fig. 2b). To visualize the polar network in the nanocomposite more directly, we performed atomic force microscopy-infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) on both the terpolymer and the nanocomposite28. In the chemical image of the terpolymer/PDs, the polar network structure was clearly visible (Fig. 2c), whereas the terpolymer lacked a polar network due to the absence of the all-trans conformation (Fig. 2d). Local infrared spectroscopy confirmed that PDs introduction indeed induces the formation of the all-trans conformation in the terpolymer (Fig. 2e and 2f). In contrast, due to all-trans conformation defects, homogeneous chemical mapping existed for the terpolymer (Fig. 2d). The thermal properties of the composites with varying PDs contents were characterized by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The second heating cycle revealed that both the melting temperature and melting enthalpy of the composite films exhibited a gradual decrease with increasing PDs content (Supplementary Fig. S3). This trend indicates that the incorporation of PDs, through hydrogen bonding, significantly influences the microstructure of the polymer matrix, likely by altering the chain packing and organization associated with the all-trans conformation. We measured the S 3 of these uniformly distributed all-trans conformation films (Supplementary Fig. S4 and S5), which were 5.6% (10 Hz) and 6.7% (1 Hz) for terpolymer/PDs and 2.5% (10 Hz) and 3.1% (1 Hz) for the pure terpolymer at 100 MV m−1. The electrostrictive performance of composites was significantly enhanced by introducing PDs. The electrostrictive strain was characterized at 1 Hz and 10 Hz to ensure direct comparability with established literature and to assess the frequency-dependent response20,21. The marginally higher strain at 1 Hz is typical of relaxor ferroelectrics, reflecting the enhanced polarization alignment at lower frequencies. The maintained performance at 10 Hz confirms the material’s capability for faster actuation, highlighting its versatility across different operational regimes. It is noteworthy that the absolute electromechanical performance of P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) can be influenced by several intrinsic and extrinsic factors, including the specific monomer ratio and film-processing history. Therefore, the most critical and rigorous assessment of any enhancement strategy is a direct comparison against a control sample prepared and characterized under identical conditions, as performed in this work. All strain data reported herein were derived from multiple parallel measurements, with error bars confirming the high reproducibility of our results. We obtained the polarization response for the terpolymers and nanocomposites under unipolar and triangular electric fields (Supplementary Fig. S6 and S7), and the slender hysteresis loops showed the relaxor ferroelectric properties of the terpolymer/PDs. The composites exhibited higher polarization than that of pure terpolymers under electric fields, and the terpolymer/PDs displayed higher polarization of 0.064 C m−2 than the terpolymer of 0.057 C m−2 under an electric field of 100 MV m−1 at 1 Hz.

Effect of polymer films with a gradient distribution of all-trans conformation on actuation strain
After clarifying the interaction between PDs and terpolymers, we analyzed the mesoscopic structure of the films with a gradient of all-trans conformation. The FT-IR spectra of the upper and lower surfaces of the terpolymer films before and after the introduction of PDs confirmed that all-trans conformations were concentrated on one side (Fig. 3a). The absorption peak intensity of the lower surface of the composite at 1286 cm−1 was significantly higher than that on the upper surface of the composite, whereas the absorption peak intensity of the lower surface of the terpolymer at 1286 cm−1 was slightly increased compared to that on the upper surface. Fig. 3b shows the grazing incidence XRD patterns of the upper and lower surfaces of terpolymers and terpolymer/PDs composites. The reflection of the lower surface of the polymer film before and after adding PDs was shifted towards a higher angle compared to the upper surface, indicating a decrease in the interchain spacing between the lower surfaces of the terpolymer and composites. The introduction of PDs increases the number of all-trans conformations, while gradual heating promotes the uneven distribution of these increased all-trans conformations. The spatial chemical analysis of the cross-sections of terpolymer-G and terpolymer/PDs-G based on AFM-IR was shown in Fig. 3c-f (laser irradiation frequency of 1286 cm−1, corresponding to all-trans conformation). Five points were selected from bottom to top on the cross-section of the materials, and local infrared spectroscopy confirmed that the cross-section of the terpolymer/PDs-G gradually decreased in all-trans conformation from bottom to top (Fig. 3e), with a slow change process rather than a sudden change. The local infrared spectrum of the cross-section of the terpolymer-G was shown in Fig. 3f, and the all-trans conformation also changed slowly. The interconnection network of polar phases can be clearly seen in the chemical image of the terpolymer/PDs-G composite (Fig. 3c). On the contrary, owing to the deficiency of all-trans conformation, homogeneous chemical mapping was present in the terpolymer (Fig. 3d). The AFM-IR of the upper and lower surfaces of the terpolymer-G films before and after the introduction of PDs more intuitively confirmed the phenomenon of concentrated distribution of all-trans conformation on one side (Supplementary Fig. S8). The polar phase was most pronounced on the lower surface of the composite film by laser irradiation at 1286 cm−1. We performed high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) on the upper and lower layers of the cross-section of the terpolymer/PDs-G composite (Fig. 3g, 3j). The fast Fourier transform indicated that the terpolymer at the interface between the lower layer of the terpolymer/PDs-G nanocomposite (Fig. 3h) exhibited more all-trans conformation than the upper layer (Fig. 3i). We compare the actuation strain of all-trans conformational changes originating from enhanced hydrogen bonding interactions in a gradient-distributed structure. Fig. 3k, S1b, and S9 show the S 3 of terpolymer/PDs-G under different electric field strengths. At 100 MV m−1, the S 3 of the terpolymer/PDs-G film reaches 13.1% at 10 Hz and 14.4% at 1 Hz, whereas that of the terpolymer-G film is only 3.0% at 10 Hz and 3.2% at 1 Hz, which is an improvement of approximately 330-350%. As shown in Fig. 3l, the terpolymer/PDs-G film exhibits the largest actuation performance when compared to inorganic, organic, and composite materials reported in the literature20,22,29–32. In addition, as the frequency increases, the peak of the dielectric constant (ε r) of the terpolymer/PDs-G film shifts to higher temperatures, indicating its relaxor ferroelectric properties (Supplementary Fig. S10). 0.5 wt% of terpolymer/PDs-G shows a higher ε r than that of terpolymer-G at 1000 Hz and room temperature, which contributes to the enhancement of its electrostrictive performance (Supplementary Fig. S11). Meanwhile, the P-E loops of the terpolymer-G and terpolymer/PDs-G nanocomposites under unipolar and bipolar electric fields (Supplementary Figs. S12 and S13) display slim hysteresis curves, further confirming their relaxor ferroelectric behavior. Moreover, under an electric field of 100 MV m−1 and a frequency of 1 Hz, the polarization of the composite material reaches 0.070 C m−2, which is higher than 0.059 C m−2 for terpolymer-G.

Electrostriction coefficient (Q 33) is a key parameter for evaluating the electrostriction properties of materials. Based on the electrostrictive strains (Fig. 3k and Supplementary Fig. S1b) and polarizations (Supplementary Fig. S12), we derived the Q 33 of nanocomposites and pristine terpolymer under different electric fields (Supplementary Fig. S14) from the equation: S 3 = Q 33 P2. Q 33 of terpolymer/PDs-G is more than twice as much as that of the terpolymer-G. At 100 MV m−1 and 1 Hz, the |Q 33 | of terpolymer/PDs-G is 44.3 m4 C−2 while that of terpolymer-G is only 10.6 m4 C−2. The electromechanical coupling factor (k 33) can be calculated from output mechanical energy with k 33 = output mechanical energy / input electrical energy33. At 100 MV m−1 and 1 Hz, the k 33 of terpolymer/PDs-G is 0.370 while that of terpolymer-G is 0.0794 (as shown in Supplementary Fig. S15). For effective operation of electric actuators, the driving material must have excellent mechanical energy density (E m) to generate sufficient force to move the load. Mechanical energy density is defined as E m = 0.5 YS² (Y, elastic modulus; S, actuation strain). The large strain and modulus (0.186 GPa) in the terpolymer/PDs-G produced 1.92 J cm−3 (Supplementary Fig. S16), which is nearly twice that of ferroelectric polymers and polymer composites, and even comparable to ferroelectric ceramics.

To investigate whether the deformation effect of protrusion or depression in composites is related to the elastic modulus of the upper and lower surfaces of the film, we measured the elastic modulus of the relatively uniform distribution of all-trans conformation before and after adding PDs (Supplementary Fig. S17). The elastic moduli of the composites were generally higher than those of the terpolymers, with the elastic moduli of the upper and lower surfaces of the terpolymer being 153 MPa and 156 MPa, respectively, while those of the terpolymer/PDs were 170 MPa and 175 MPa for the upper and lower surfaces of the terpolymer/PDs, respectively. The elastic modulus of the materials with a uniform distribution of the all-trans conformations was slightly higher for their lower surfaces than for their upper surfaces. Supplementary Fig. S18 showed the elastic modulus of the upper and lower surfaces of films with all-trans conformation gradient distribution before and after the addition of PDs. The elastic moduli of the upper and lower surfaces of the terpolymer-G were 163 MPa and 167 MPa, respectively, while the elastic moduli of the upper and lower surfaces of the terpolymer/PDs-G composites were 183 MPa and 189 MPa, respectively. The differences in elastic modulus between the upper and lower surfaces of the two were similar to those of terpolymers and composites with a uniform distribution of all-trans conformation. The composites with a gradient distribution of all-trans conformation can realize unidirectional bending actuation. Therefore, the deformation effect of composites that can achieve protrusion or depression was mainly related to the gradient distribution of all-trans conformation, but not to the elastic modulus of the upper and lower surfaces. This asymmetry between the upper and lower surfaces caused the polymer composite to form a structure similar to that of a classic unimorph device, allowing the single-layer polymer film to bend under an electric field. Leveraging this unique characteristic, we have developed a complete caterpillars-to-butterflies biomimetic robotics system.

The manufacture and performance of the caterpillars-to-butterflies bionic actuation system
Nanocomposites with a gradient structure have excellent actuation properties because they form a natural single deformation. The actuator made of this nanocomposite has the potential to create insect-size robots. The breakdown strength of terpolymers and nanocomposites is shown in Supplementary Fig. S20. The introduction of PDs increases the breakdown strength by about 27 MV m−1 to 249 MV m−1. To gain deeper insight into the mechanism behind the enhanced dielectric breakdown strength, we employed thermally-stimulated depolarization current (TSDC) and leakage current measurements (Supplementary Fig. S21 and S22). The TSDC spectrum of the terpolymer/PDs-G composite revealed a main relaxation peak shifted to a higher temperature (24.9 °C) compared to that of the pure terpolymer-G (23.8 °C), indicating the presence of deepened energy traps for charge carriers, which we attribute to the strong hydrogen-bonded interfaces. Furthermore, the composite exhibited a lower leakage current density than the pure polymer under high electric fields (Supplementary Fig. S22). These findings collectively demonstrate that the PDs, via hydrogen bonding, create effective charge traps that suppress charge injection and transport. This suppressed conduction is a key factor in delaying the onset of dielectric breakdown, thereby contributing to the breakdown strength and reliability of the composite. When fabricating dielectric devices, breakdown strength is a critical material property metric, requiring that the applied electric field remain below 20% of the breakdown strength20. For actuators fabricated from our materials, actuation performance at an electric field below 50 MV m−¹ is particularly crucial.

The upper surface of the terpolymer/PDs-G was placed upward, as shown in Fig. 4a. The composite was made into a shape similar to that of a caterpillar. The head and tail of the caterpillar are sharper and narrower compared to the abdomen. A slightly wider abdomen provides sufficient power while crawling, and the head and tail are designed with symmetrical circular arcs to reduce the resistance of the caterpillar to extend and stretch its body during the crawling process. The electrode coating is applied in the middle of the material, and the elliptical electrode was designed to ensure the stable crawling of the caterpillar during the crawling process. The crawling route is designed as a bumpy ladder structure, which is more in line with the various complex road conditions encountered by caterpillars during their survival in nature. Supplementary Fig. S19a shows the complete morphology of the crawling device. In the presence of an electric field, the caterpillars can steadily crawl at a peristaltic frequency of 2 Hz. The caterpillar crawled a distance of 9 cm in 2 s, with a crawling speed of up to 4.5 cm s−1. The operating voltage and current are shown in Supplementary Fig. S23, and the single-cycle energy consumption can be calculated (W = UIt, U, single-cycle voltage; I, single-cycle current; t, single-cycle elapsed time). The single-cycle energy consumption is only 9.04 × 10−4 J. We recorded the crawling process using a high-speed camera (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Movie 2).

In contrast to the above process, by changing the shape of the film and control conditions, going through such a cocooning process, we also produced a bionic butterfly flight actuator from this material. As shown in Fig. 4a, the composite was made to resemble the shape of a butterfly. The head and tail of the butterfly were designed in a streamlined shape. The reason for the small, curved, streamlined shape of the head is that it carries the head of the butterfly when the wings swing upward. Then, when the wings were swung downward, the large, curved, streamlined shape of the tail was designed to allow the butterfly to take off from the ground. We coated the electrodes in the middle area of the material and designed the electrode area in an elliptical shape because the elliptical active area was more conducive to driving the wings on both sides. In the presence of an electric field, the wings achieved reversible flapping behavior. The operating voltage and current are shown in Supplementary Fig. S24, and single-cycle energy consumption was only 4.99 × 10−4 J. Supplementary Fig. S25a shows the complete morphology of the flight device. We recorded the actuation process using a high-speed camera (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Movies 3 and 4). Without any additional auxiliary equipment, the active actuation area in the center of the film alone can carry up to 20 times its own weight, allowing the flight device to reach a height of 2-4 mm above the ground. To precisely evaluate its actuation performance, we systematically characterized the variation of the angular displacement of the butterfly wing with the applied electric field. We systematically characterized the angular displacement of the butterfly wing as a function of the applied electric field (Supplementary Fig. S26). As shown in Supplementary Movie 5, the actuator demonstrates rapid, reversible, and highly repeatable flapping behavior under a 1 Hz electric field. The flipping angle of the wing steadily increases with the electric field strength. Quantitative data reveal that the angular displacement grows from a slight movement at low fields to a substantial angle of approximately 90° at an electric field of 50 MV m−1. This significant angular displacement not only visually confirms the success of our gradient design in amplifying local high strain into effective macroscopic motion but also signifies that this all-organic actuator has reached a state-of-the-art level in its output capability.

The two insect-sized actuators are lightweight. The bionic caterpillar actuator weighs 55.4 mg, and the bionic butterfly actuator weighs 44.8 mg. As shown in the Table S1, both actuators are significantly lighter than those reported in existing studies3,17,34–40, demonstrating a substantial weight advantage for their class. To quantitatively evaluate the energy efficiency of our actuators, we calculated the input power per cycle from the recorded voltage and current transients during operation, defined as P = W/t (W, single-cycle energy consumption; t, single-cycle elapsed time). The most rigorous validation of our material strategy comes from a direct comparison under identical actuator designs. We fabricated bio-inspired caterpillars and butterflies using both the terpolymer/PDs-G composite and the control terpolymer-G. Remarkably, to achieve a comparable actuation strain, the terpolymer/PDs-G actuator requires a driving field of only 30 MV m−1, whereas the terpolymer-G actuator necessitates 100 MV m−1 (Fig. 3k). Their operating voltage and current are shown in Supplementary Figs. S27 and S28, and their motion behavior is depicted in Supplementary Movies 6 and 7. This drastic reduction in the required operating field directly translates to a substantial decrease in input power. Specifically, the input power for the terpolymer/PDs-G caterpillar actuator is 2.532 mW, which is an order of magnitude lower than the 26.32 mW required by the terpolymer-G caterpillar at their respective driving fields. A similar power reduction was confirmed for the butterfly actuators (5.248 mW vs. 57.94 mW). This internal comparison provides definitive evidence that our composite material enables ultra-low power consumption. Furthermore, compared with other reported electric soft actuators (Fig. 4d, Table S1)3,17,34–38,41,42, our terpolymer/PDs-G actuators (consuming 3.62 mW and 7.98 mW at higher performance regimes) also demonstrate highly competitive, low input power, underscoring their overall efficiency and practical potential. The achievement of two locomotion modes using a single material with ultra-low energy consumption allows for a targeted approach to meet different needs, which is unprecedented. The composite has enormous application value in the field of soft robot actuation and provides ideas for the profound development of sensors.

While this work demonstrates that our single-layer, gradient composite actuator achieves exceptional performance in terms of strain, low mass (~50 mg), and ultra-low input power (on the order of milliwatts), we acknowledge that its current operational framework requires a high driving voltage (~1.5 kV). This requirement for an external high-voltage source presents a recognized challenge for the development of fully untethered, autonomous soft robots, as it necessitates ancillary power conversion circuitry. The core trade-off in our present design is indeed the achievement of a simplified, monolithic fabrication process and high electromechanical performance at the cost of operational voltage. However, it is crucial to distinguish between operating voltage and input power. The low power claim central to this work refers to the minimal energy consumption (in mW) during operation, a metric in which our actuators are highly competitive, as benchmarked in Table S1. This low power consumption, combined with the exceptionally low mass of the active material itself, is a critical step toward future energy-autonomous systems. The single-material, unimorph architecture eliminates interfacial energy losses common in multi-layer laminates and is the direct cause of the low mass and simple structure that enable complex biomimetic motions. Future work will squarely focus on overcoming the voltage limitation, through strategies such as developing much thinner films or exploring multi-layer co-fabrication to reduce the required driving voltage to more practical levels without compromising the achieved benefits of low mass and power.
paper_content.methods:
Materials
P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) terpolymer with the composition of VDF/TrFE/CFE = 61.2/31.3/7.5 mol% was obtained from Piezo Technologies, France. N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Citric acid (CA) was obtained from Aladdin, and ethylenediamine (EDA) was received from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent co., Ltd. All the chemicals were used as received.

Synthesis of polymer dots
In this work, the PDs were prepared following a classical bottom-up method, hydrothermal crosslinking24, as shown in the Supplementary Fig. S29. CA (1.0507 g) and EDA (335 µL) were initially dissolved in deionized water (10 mL). Then the mixed solution was transferred to a poly(tetrafluoroethylene) (Teflon)-lined autoclave (30 mL) and heated at 180 °C for 7 h, the reactors were naturally cooled to room temperature. At the end of the reaction, the solution was transferred to a dialysis bag for 30 h. After dialysis, the solution was freeze-dried for 72 h to obtain brown PDs. Finally, the brown-black powders PDs were obtained (Supplementary Figs. S30–S32, Supplementary Information for relevant characterization of PDs).

Polymer/polymer dots (PDs) composite films preparation
In the preparation of the composite films (terpolymer/PDs-G) shown in Supplementary Fig. S33, 0.3 g of terpolymer was dissolved in 5 mL DMF and stirred overnight at room temperature. Depending on the required mass fraction in the composites, the appropriate weight of PDs was dissolved in 3 mL of DMF and sonicated for 1 h before using. These homogeneous solutions were then dropped onto a 6 cm × 6 cm clean glass slide and placed in an oven at 60 °C for 4 h, then the temperature was slowly raised to 120 °C within 8 h. Afterward, the polymer films were placed in a vacuum oven and annealed at 120 °C for 12 h (corresponding to a controlled ramp rate of 7.5 °C h−1). The thickness of the films was in the range of 30 μm to 40 μm. The distribution of characteristic elements in terpolymers and composites was characterized by energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), as shown in Supplementary Fig. S32. The appearance of the O element in the EDS image of the composite indicates the successful introduction of PDs into the terpolymer, and the uniform distribution of elements suggests the uniformity of the composites. The terpolymer/PDs films with uniformly distributed all-trans conformation were treated at 60-120 °C for 12 h during the preparation process to evaporate the solvent, and the other treatment methods were the same as the above process for terpolymer/PDs-G.

The fabrication and construction of the bionic caterpillar crawling actuator and the bionic butterfly flight actuator
The prepared polymer composite film was cut into homogeneous texture according to the shape and size as shown in Supplementary Figs. S34 and S35 and carbon nanotubes (CNT, XFNANO, purity > 90%, 1–2 nm in diameter and 1–3 µm in length) were deposited on the surface of the composite film by spray-coating (Dahua, DH350E) to form the elliptical shaped active area as electrodes, and the active area was extended to the upper and lower edges of the film through elongated conductive regions, respectively. The ultra-thin copper strips (0.06 mm in thickness) were attached onto the composite film with conductive adhesive to serve as a skeleton support, and connected to the high-voltage power supply through ultrafine copper wires (0.03 mm in diameter). In the bionic caterpillar crawling actuator, we designed the crawling route as a stepped structure with a slope of 40° and a length of 90 mm to simulate the rough tree-like structure in nature. Specific details can be seen in Supplementary Fig. S19, Supplementary Movie 2. For the bionic butterfly flight actuator, in order to avoid the impact of the force generated by the wings flapping on the ground on the mechanical and electrical performance display of the composites, all flight tests were conducted on narrow glass platforms, with a 1 cm small square set in the center of the glass platform to slightly sink the active area of the flight actuator, allowing the wings to be upwardly folded (Supplementary Fig. S25 and Supplementary Movies 3 and 4).

Characterizations and measurements
The SEM experiment was captured on a JEOL JSM-7401F scanning electron microscope with an EDS analysis attachment. The TEM and HRTEM images were obtained by a JEM-2100F instrument. The films were embedded in epoxy resin and then sectioned using an EM UC7 ultramicrotome. Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) measurement was carried out on a Varian Digilab FTS-8010 spectrophotometer. Peak Force Quantitative Nanomechanical Mapping (PFQNM) characterizations of surface elastic modulus were measured by Multimode 8. AFM-IR measurements were obtained from a Bruker Anasys nanoIR3 system. Simultaneous acquisition of topographic and chemical images by tapping mode. The HRTEM images were captured on a JEM-2100F transmission electron microscope. A UV2501-PC spectrophotometer was used to get Ultraviolet-visible (UV-vis) absorption spectra. Two-dimensional (2D) glancing incidence experiments were performed at the Xeuss 3.0. Dielectric constants and dissipation factors were measured using an Alpha-A High Performance Frequency Analyzer, and the samples (diameter 3.4 mm and thickness about 30-40 μm) were deposited on a 30 nm thick copper. The polarization-electric field (P-E) loops were collected using a Polarization Loop & Dielectric Breakdown Test System from PolyK, where AC electric fields with an increment of 10 MV m−1 were applied across polymer films with a triangular waveform at a frequency of 1 Hz and 10 Hz. Leakage current density was acquired from a Keithley Model 6517A electrometer equipped with a Trek Model 610C amplifier. Thermally stimulated depolarization current (TSDC) was measured by a Keithley 6517A electrometer. The samples were firstly polarized under 20 MV m−1 at 40 °C for 20 minutes a Trek Model 610C amplifier. Then the temperature was quickly dropped to -10 °C with the electric field on. After that, the samples were disconnected from the electric field and short-circuited for 2 minutes. Finally, the samples were heated from -10 °C to 60 °C at a rate of 1 °C min−1 and the current was recorded. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) data was collected by a DSC Q2000 with a heating rate of 10 °C min−1. High-speed camera images and movies were captured by the SONY DSC-RX10III digital camera. High voltage was provided by a high-voltage power supply (Dongwen, DW-P103-0). The electrostrictive strain (thickness deformation) of the films was measured using a non-contact photonic sensor system (MTI-2100 Fotonic Sensor, 2032R probe). As illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S36, the sample was placed between parallel plate electrodes, and the thickness change was measured perpendicularly by the probe. The reported strain values were recorded at 0.1 s or 1 s after field application to ensure the capture of steady-state response.

Data availability
The data generated in this study are provided in the Supplementary Information/Source Data file. All data are available from the corresponding author upon request. Source data are provided with this paper.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript presents a highly innovative and well-executed study that explores a promising strategy for developing high-performance soft actuators based on a relaxor ferroelectric polymer nanocomposite. This work offers significant potential for advancing the fields of soft robotics and insect-scale actuation systems. With some minor revisions and clarifications, this manuscript would make a valuable contribution to its area. I am pleased to recommend this manuscript for acceptance. Detailed comments and suggestions are provided below:
1. The choice of the relaxor ferroelectric polymer P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) as the matrix should be justified by explaining its relevance to the material design strategy and actuator performance.
2. A more detailed description of the strain measurement setup is needed. The authors should specify the methods and instrumentation used to quantify strain, and it would be very helpful to include schematic diagrams and/or photographs of the measurement setup for clarity and reproducibility.
3. The electrical measurements throughout the manuscript are conducted at 10 Hz and 1 Hz. The reason for explaining the rationale behind selecting these two specific frequencies should be given. A brief discussion of how the frequency affects actuator performance would strengthen the interpretation of the results.
4. The exceptional actuator performance is a key strength of this work, and the manuscript would benefit from a more thorough description of the electrode design. Specifically, details such as the dimensions, materials, and placement of the ultra-thin copper strips and ultrafine copper wires should be provided to offer a more complete and vivid picture of the device architecture.
5. The slight enhancement in the breakdown strength of the composite material is an interesting observation. Possible explanation or hypothesis for this improvement is encouraged to provide, which may further reinforce the understanding of the structure–property relationship in the composite system.
6. The article mentions achieving a gradient distribution of PDs through gradual heating at 60-120 °C, but does not specify the heating rate.It is recommended to supplement the specific heating process to improve process repeatability.
7. Why does the difference in solvent evaporation rates result in a higher proportion of all-trans conformations in the lower layer?
8. The article shows that the material performs best at 0.5 wt% PDs. Please explain why the material's performance declines when the PDs content exceeds 0.5 wt% and provide relevant supporting materials.
9. Please provide the DSC test results for pure terpolymers (terpolymer-G) and composite materials with different PDs contents (terpolymer/PDs-G).
10. Please check the chart information in fig.2 e-f.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript, "Biomimetic actuator crafted from a relaxor ferroelectric polymer nanocomposite," presents the fabrication of a single-layer actuator based on a P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) terpolymer with a gradient distribution of polymer dots (PDs). The authors claim that this novel structure leads to a functional unimorph actuator with exceptionally high strain (14.4% at 100 MV/m) and ultra-low power consumption (3-8 mW), demonstrating its potential through caterpillar-like and butterfly-like soft robots. While the concept of creating a functional gradient within a single material is intriguing and the demonstrated actuators are visually impressive, the reviewer has several major concerns regarding the experimental design, the interpretation of the results, and the validity of the central claims. These concerns are significant enough to undermine the core conclusions of the study.
1. The abstract prominently features an "exceptionally high strain" of 14.4%. This is a misleading representation of the actuator's performance. The reported value is the thickness strain (S3), which is an indirect, internal material response, not the functional output of the device. For a bending actuator, the useful performance is defined by macroscopic motion, such as bending curvature, tip deflection, or angular displacement. The high thickness strain is merely the cause that, due to the engineered gradient structure, gets converted into bending. Presenting the cause as the primary performance metric in the abstract, without this critical context, conflates an intrinsic material property with a structural amplification effect. It creates the false impression that the material itself linearly contracts or expands by this magnitude, which is not the case. This is a significant overstatement of the material's direct actuation capability.
2. The authors claim a significant material innovation, stating that the addition of PDs doubles the electrostrictive strain of the terpolymer (from ~3% to 6.7% for uniform films at 100 MV/m, Fig. S2). However, the baseline performance of their control sample (pure terpolymer-G, ~3% strain at 100 MV/m) appears to be considerably lower than what is commonly reported in the literature for this class of terpolymers, where strains of 5% or higher at 100 MV/m are typical [1]. This raises a critical question about the validity of the baseline. By using a potentially underperforming control sample, the claimed two-fold improvement due to PDs may be an overestimation. The authors must compare their results against well-established literature values or provide a compelling reason for their low baseline performance to substantiate their claim of material innovation.
3. The claim of "ultra-low power consumption" is a cornerstone of the paper, but the comparison presented in Fig. 4d and Table S1 is fundamentally flawed. The authors compare their electrostrictive actuator to actuators based on entirely different physical mechanisms (e.g., thermal, chemical, phase-change). This is not a scientifically valid. The only rigorous comparison would be against an actuator of the same design and scale fabricated from the pure terpolymer control material, which is absent from the manuscript. Without this direct comparison, the claim that their specific material/process innovation leads to an order-of-magnitude reduction in power consumption is unsubstantiated. This appears to be a case of "cherry-picking" data from disparate fields to make the results seem more significant than they are.
4. The authors frame their "single-process" approach as a major breakthrough over conventional multi-layer, laminated actuators. However, the core trade-off they have made is to simplify the fabrication process at the cost of requiring an extremely high operating voltage. The reported operating field of ~42 MV/m for a 35 µm thick film translates to a driving voltage of approximately 1.5 kV, and the fields for maximum strain (100 MV/m) require 3.5 kV. Such high kV-level voltages are a fatal flaw for the target application of small-scale, untethered biomimetic robots. It necessitates bulky, heavy, and inefficient voltage amplification circuitry, which negates the benefits of a lightweight actuator and contradicts the practical meaning of "low power." While other methods (e.g., multilayering) have more complex fabrication, they successfully address this critical voltage issue, enabling operation at much lower and more practical voltages (<100 V). The authors' failure to acknowledge and discuss this severe limitation, while heavily emphasizing the process simplification, makes the claims of practical advancement feel unbalanced and misleading. The innovation is not the simplification of the process itself, but rather the creation of a functional unimorph structure. However, the practical viability of this structure is highly questionable due to the voltage requirements.
In summary, the manuscript's central claims of significant material improvement, ultra-low power consumption, and practical innovation are built on a foundation of questionable baselines, inappropriate comparisons, and the omission of a critical discussion on the impracticality of the high operating voltage. While the idea is interesting, the work in its current form does not provide sufficient rigorous and contextual evidence to support its claims. Therefore, the reviewer regrets that the reviewer cannot recommend this manuscript for publication.
Reference
[1] S. Zhang, C. Huang, Z.-Y. Cheng, F. Xia, R. Klein, Q. M. Zhang, V. Bobnar, A. Levstik, and F. Bauer, Relaxor Ferroelectric Polymers, Ferroelectrics, 339:37–45, 2006. (DOI: 10.1080/00150190600737917)
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, the authors reported multi-mode soft actuators with low power consumption of 3-8 mW but high loading weight up to 2000% of its own weight, which was achieved using a monolayer all-organic nanocomposite with gradually distributed polymer dots (PDs). They found the proportion of all-trans conformations in the terpolymer was increased by the hydrogen bonding between the functional groups on the PD surface and the fluorine atoms in the terpolymer chains, resulting a gradient distribution of the high-polarization moiety. Notably, the nanocomposite film exhibited ultrahigh electrostriction performance with maximum strain of 14.4% and an output mechanical energy density of 1.92 J cm-3 at 100 MV m-1. This finding represents a significant advancement in in ferroelectric polymers and soft actuators, paving the way to truly bionic soft robots. I strongly recommend the publication of this nice work in Nature Communications after some minor revisions.
1. In the paper, the theoretical rationale for selecting the relaxor ferroelectric polymer P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) as the matrix and polymer dots as the filler should be systematically and clearly elaborated. This section should not only include the fundamental characteristics of the materials themselves but also provide a detailed explanation of the intrinsic relationship between their structure and properties—such as the high dielectric constant and remarkable electrostrictive effect of P(VDF-TrFE-CFE), as well as the unique advantages of polymer dots in interface modification and dielectric enhancement. Providing sufficient and clear background information will help readers gain a deeper understanding of the scientific logic behind the material selection and establish the structure-property relationship between these choices and the final actuator performance (e.g., strain output, energy density), thereby enhancing the scientific rigor and persuasiveness of the paper.
2. The gradual distribution of polymer dots (PDs) in the monolayer all-organic nanocomposite is the highlight of this work. What is the driving force of this gradual distribution? Gradual heating temperature-rise periods. Or the graded distribution of temperatures in the films on the heating plate, where temperatures decrease from the bottom to the top.
3. Is the "gradual heating process" discussed in the paper straightforward to standardize? How consistent are results from one batch to the next? Are there any data to back up its process stability?
4. The authors assert that the incorporation of polymer dots leads to an enhanced breakdown strength. It is recommended that they provide potential explanations or hypotheses for this observed improvement, thereby facilitating a more profound understanding of the structure-property relationship within the composite system. Furthermore, the authors should consider performing leakage current and/or thermally stimulated depolarization current (TSDC) measurements to substantiate these findings.
5. The outstanding performance of the actuator is a principal highlight of this research. To facilitate a deeper reader understanding of the device's structure-property relationship, a more detailed description of the actuator's design is recommended. Furthermore, more thorough elucidation of the strain measurement process, including the methodologies, pertinent parameters, and fundamental principles, is advised. This will significantly augment reader comprehension of the measurement approach and streamline the reproducibility of the experimental protocol.
6. Please check the text in Fig. 2e, f. According to the caption, e is terpolymer/PDs，f is terpolymer. Please confirm it.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Answers to the Comments
We would first like to express our gratitude to the reviewers for their insightful comments, which helped us further improve this manuscript. Detailed responses to the comments are as follows:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript presents a highly innovative and well-executed study that explores a promising strategy for developing high-performance soft actuators based on a relaxor ferroelectric polymer nanocomposite. This work offers significant potential for advancing the fields of soft robotics and insect-scale actuation systems. With some minor revisions and clarifications, this manuscript would make a valuable contribution to its area. I am pleased to recommend this manuscript for acceptance. Detailed comments and suggestions are provided below:
1. The choice of the relaxor ferroelectric polymer P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) as the matrix should be justified by explaining its relevance to the material design strategy and actuator performance.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree that a more detailed explanation of the material selection rationale will significantly strengthen the manuscript and provide readers with a deeper understanding of the structure-property correlations in our system. We have thoroughly revised the introduction section to provide a systematic and explicit elaboration as suggested.
Rationale for P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) Matrix: We now elaborate on its unique molecular structure. The incorporation of CFE monomers into the P(VDF-TrFE) lattice disrupts the long-range ferroelectric order, creating nano-polar regions that are highly responsive to electric fields. This structure is responsible for the material's high dielectric constant and relaxor ferroelectric behavior, characterized by a large electric-field-induced polarization with minimal hysteresis – a fundamental requirement for high-performance electrostrictive actuators.
To address the Reviewer’s suggestion,
These additions have been integrated into the introduction of the revised manuscript (Page 3).
“The incorporation of CFE monomers into the P(VDF-TrFE) lattice disrupts the long-range ferroelectric order, creating nano-polar regions that are highly responsive to electric fields. This structure is responsible for the high dielectric constant and relaxor ferroelectric behavior of the material, characterized by a large electric-field-induced polarization with minimal hysteresis, which is a fundamental requirement for high-performance electrostrictive actuators.”
2. A more detailed description of the strain measurement setup is needed. The authors should specify the methods and instrumentation used to quantify strain, and it would be very helpful to include schematic diagrams and/or photographs of the measurement setup for clarity and reproducibility.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion to improve the clarity of our experimental methods. We have thoroughly revised the "Experimental Section" to provide a more detailed description of the strain measurement setup.
We characterized the electrostrictive strain (deformation in the thickness direction) of the polymer films using a non-contact photonic sensor system (MTI-2100 Fotonic Sensor with a 2032R probe). This method offers high-resolution displacement measurement, which is critical for accurately quantifying the small deformations in thin films. A schematic diagram of the measurement setup is provided in Fig. R1, and a photograph of the actual instrument is shown in Fig. R2. The film sample was placed between two parallel plate electrodes, with the photonic sensor probe aligned perpendicularly to measure the thickness change. Upon application of the electric field, the temporal evolution of the displacement was recorded. The reported electrostrictive strain values were determined after the signal had stabilized, typically at 0.1 s or 1 s after the field was applied, ensuring the measurement captured the steady-state material response rather than any transient effects.
Fig. R1 Schematic of a photonic sensor setup for the longitudinal strain measurement.
Fig. R2 The physical photo of the photonic sensor setup for the longitudinal strain measurement.
To address the Reviewer’s suggestion,
The measure instrument, measure method and related test details of electroactuation strains were supplemented in the Materials and Methods section of the revised manuscript. And we have supplemented Fig. S36 in the revised Supplementary Information and marked in red.
“The electrostrictive strain (thickness deformation) of the films was measured using a non-contact photonic sensor system (MTI-2100 Fotonic Sensor, 2032R probe). As illustrated in Fig. S36, the sample was placed between parallel plate electrodes, and thickness change was measured perpendicularly by the probe. The reported strain values were recorded at 0.1 s or 1 s after field application to ensure the capture of steady-state response.”
Fig. S36 Schematic of a photonic sensor setup for the longitudinal strain measurement.
3. The electrical measurements throughout the manuscript are conducted at 10 Hz and 1 Hz. The reason for explaining the rationale behind selecting these two specific frequencies should be given. A brief discussion of how the frequency affects actuator performance would strengthen the interpretation of the results.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. Our reasons for selecting 1 Hz and 10 Hz are twofold:
Ensuring Broad Comparability: These frequencies are widely adopted standards in the field of relaxor ferroelectric polymers. Some key studies focus on 1 Hz1, while others, including seminal works, utilize 10 Hz2. By presenting data at both frequencies, we provide a direct and meaningful basis for comparison with a broader body of literature, allowing readers to better contextualize the performance of our material.
Probing Material Dynamics: The choice of frequency allows us to assess the dynamic electromechanical response of our material. As expected for relaxor ferroelectric polymers, a lower driving frequency (1 Hz) provides a longer period for dipole switching and domain wall motion, often resulting in a marginally higher measured strain compared to a higher frequency (10 Hz). The slight decrease in strain observed at 10 Hz (as seen in our Fig. S3) can be attributed to the inertia of the polar nanoregions and increased viscous losses within the polymer matrix at shorter time scales.
This frequency-dependent behavior is not just a metric but has practical implications for actuator design. The performance at 1 Hz is highly relevant for applications requiring larger strains in quasi-static or slow-cycle operations (e.g., robotic gripping, crawling). Conversely, the performance maintained at 10 Hz demonstrates the material's capability for faster, more dynamic actuation (e.g., flapping, vibration control), highlighting its versatility. We agree with the reviewer that this discussion strengthens the paper, and we are grateful for the suggestion to include it.
To address the Reviewer’s suggestion,
We have now added the rationale for frequency selection and a discussion on frequency dependence to the revised manuscript (Page 7).
“The electrostrictive strain was characterized at 1 Hz and 10 Hz to ensure direct comparability with established literature and to assess the frequency-dependent response 1,2. The marginally higher strain at 1 Hz is typical of relaxor ferroelectrics, reflecting the enhanced polarization alignment at lower frequencies. The maintained performance at 10 Hz confirms the material's capability for faster actuation, highlighting its versatility across different operational regimes.”
4. The exceptional actuator performance is a key strength of this work, and the manuscript would benefit from a more thorough description of the electrode design. Specifically, details such as the dimensions, materials, and placement of the ultra-thin copper strips and ultrafine copper wires should be provided to offer a more complete and vivid picture of the device architecture.
We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion to improve the clarity of our device fabrication. In direct response, we have now revised the " Materials and Methods Section" in the manuscript to include the specific details regarding the electrode and structural support components.
The prepared polymer composite film was cut into the desired shapes (Fig. S34 and S35). Carbon nanotubes (CNT, XFNANO, purity > 90%, 1-2 nm in diameter and 1-3 µm in length) were spray-coated (Dahua, DH-350E) onto the film surface to form the elliptical active electrode area, with elongated conductive regions extending to the upper and lower edges. Ultra-thin copper strips (0.06 mm in thickness) were attached using conductive adhesive to serve as a skeletal support and current collector. These strips were then connected to the high-voltage power supply via ultrafine copper wires (0.03 mm in diameter).
This revision explicitly includes the materials (copper), key dimensions (thickness and diameter), and the specific roles (skeletal support and electrical connection) of these components. We believe this addition offers a vivid and complete depiction of our actuator design, directly addressing your comment.
To address the Reviewer’s suggestion,
The modified text can be found on Page 19 of the revised manuscript and has been highlighted for your convenience.
“The prepared polymer composite film was cut into homogeneous texture according to the shape and size as shown in Fig. S34 and Fig. S35. And carbon nanotubes (CNT, XFNANO, purity > 90%, 1-2 nm in diameter and 1-3 µm in length) were deposited on the surface of the composite film by spray-coating (Dahua, DH350E) to form the elliptical shaped active area as electrodes, and the active area was extended to the upper and lower edges of the film through elongated conductive regions, respectively. The ultra-thin copper strips (0.06 mm in thickness) were attached onto the composite film with conductive adhesive to serve as a skeleton support, and connected to the high-voltage power supply through ultrafine copper wires (0.03 mm in diameter).”
5. The slight enhancement in the breakdown strength of the composite material is an interesting observation. Possible explanation or hypothesis for this improvement is encouraged to provide, which may further reinforce the understanding of the structure–property relationship in the composite system.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. Following the reviewer's advice, we have conducted both thermal-stimulated depolarization current (TSDC) and leakage current measurements on the pure terpolymer-G and the terpolymer/PDs-G composite. The results provide profound insights into the underlying mechanism of breakdown strength enhancement, which we have elaborated in the revised manuscript. Our findings and proposed explanations are summarized as follows:
1) TSDC Analysis: Revealing Deepened Charge Traps and Interface Polarization
The TSDC curves offer direct evidence of how PDs modify the charge trapping landscape and polarization behavior within the composite (Fig. R3):
Shift of Main Relaxation Peak: The main relaxation peak of the composite (terpolymer/PDs-G) shifts to a higher temperature (24.9 °C) compared to that of the pure terpolymer-G (23.8 °C). In TSDC, a shift to a higher temperature indicates that a greater amount of energy is required to release the trapped charges. We attribute this to the strong hydrogen bonding between the PDs and the terpolymer matrix. These interfacial hydrogen bonds act as deep, stable traps for space charges, immobilizing them and preventing their early activation and long-range migration.
Emergence of a New Low-Temperature Peak: A distinct new peak appears at ~2.6 °C in the terpolymer/PDs-G composite, which is absent in the pure polymer. This new peak is attributed to the interface-induced polarization. The abundant PDs/terpolymer interfaces, coupled with the hydrogen bonding, create new interfacial polarization modes. These modes are activated at lower temperatures and contribute to the overall polarizability of the material without leading to destructive charge conduction.
Increase in Total Polarization (Peak Area): The total depolarization charge, which is proportional to the area under the TSDC curve, is larger for the terpolymer/PDs-G composite. This confirms that the composite can store a greater amount of polarized charge under an electric field. The synergistic effect of the intrinsic dipolar relaxation of the terpolymer and the newly introduced interfacial polarization leads to this enhanced charge storage capability.
Fig. R3 TSDC curves of (a) terpolymer-G and (b) terpolymer/PDs-G.
2) Leakage Current Analysis: Direct Evidence of Suppressed Charge Transport
The leakage current measurement provides a direct link between the TSDC findings and the macroscopic dielectric strength (Fig. R4):
The terpolymer/PDs-G composite exhibits a slightly reduced leakage current density compared to the pure terpolymer-G. This result directly validates the role of PDs as effective charge traps. The deep traps revealed by TSDC effectively capture and immobilize charge carriers that are injected under a high electric field. By suppressing the formation of a conductive path, these trapped charges prevent the rapid increase of leakage current, thereby delaying the onset of breakdown strength and enhancing the overall dielectric strength of the material.
Fig. R4 The leakage current density of the terpolymer-G and the terpolymer/PDs-G.
To address the Reviewer’s suggestion,
We have incorporated these new TSDC and leakage current data, along with the above discussion, into the revised manuscript (Page 13) to strengthen our claim. The relevant test instructions for TSDC and leakage current have been supplemented in the Materials and Methods section and marked in red. The TSDC curves and the leakage current test data have been added to the revised Supplementary Fig. S21 and Fig. S22.
“To gain deeper insight into the mechanism behind the enhanced dielectric breakdown strength, we employed thermal-stimulated depolarization current (TSDC) and leakage current measurements (Fig. S21 and Fig. S22). The TSDC spectrum of the terpolymer/PDs-G composite revealed a main relaxation peak shifted to a higher temperature (24.9 °C) compared to that of the pure terpolymer-G (23.8 °C), indicating the presence of deepened energy traps for charge carriers, which we attribute to the strong hydrogen-bonded interfaces. Furthermore, the composite exhibited a lower leakage current density than the pure polymer under high electric fields (Fig. S22). These findings collectively demonstrate that the PDs, via hydrogen bonding, create effective charge traps that suppress charge injection and transport. This suppressed conduction is a key factor in delaying the onset of dielectric breakdown, thereby contributing to the breakdown strength and reliability of the composite.”
Materials and Methods:
“Leakage current density was acquired from Keithley Model 6517A electrometer equipped with a Trek Model 610C amplifier. Thermally stimulated depolarization current (TSDC) was measured by a Keithley 6517A electrometer. The samples were firstly polarized under 20 MV m-1 at 40 °C for 20 minutes a Trek Model 610C amplifier. Then the temperature was quickly dropped to -10 °C with the electric field on. After that, the samples were disconnected from the electric field and short-circuited for 2 minutes. Finally, the samples were heated from -10 °C to 60 °C at a rate of 1 °C min-1 and the current was recorded.”
Fig. S21 TSDC curves of (a) terpolymer-G and (b) terpolymer/PDs-G.
Fig. S22 The leakage current density of the terpolymer-G and the terpolymer/PDs-G.
6. The article mentions achieving a gradient distribution of PDs through gradual heating at 60-120 °C, but does not specify the heating rate. It is recommended to supplement the specific heating process to improve process repeatability.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion to improve the reproducibility of our method. We have now revised the corresponding section in the "Experimental Section" of the manuscript to explicitly state the heating rate.
The original description stated the film was placed in an oven at 60 °C for 4 h, and then the temperature was "slowly raised to 120 °C within 8 h." To eliminate any ambiguity, we have revised this sentence for precision. The updated text now reads:
"...placed in an oven at 60 °C for 4 h, and then the temperature was raised to 120 °C over 8 h (corresponding to a controlled ramp rate of 7.5 °C h-1)..."
This clarification provides the specific heating rate used in our process, which we agree is essential for ensuring the repeatability of gradient formation. The modification has been made on Page 19 of the revised manuscript.
7. Why does the difference in solvent evaporation rates result in a higher proportion of all-trans conformations in the lower layer ?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this profound question regarding the core physical mechanism. The higher proportion of all-trans conformations at the bottom layer is a direct consequence of the slower solvent evaporation rate there, which is governed by the principles of polymer crystallization kinetics. The key lies in the competition between the timescales of chain mobility and solvent removal:
At the Bottom Surface (Slower Evaporation): The film's bottom is in direct contact with the hot substrate. While the absolute temperature is higher, the solvent concentration remains high for a longer duration, plasticizing the polymer chains and granting them high mobility. This prolonged "wet" state provides ample time for the polymer chains to undergo conformational rearrangement, align, and pack into the thermodynamically more stable, extended all-trans conformation.
At the Top Surface (Faster Evaporation): The top surface loses solvent rapidly into the air, especially as the oven temperature increases. This quickly increases the polymer concentration and viscosity, effectively "freezing" the polymer chains in place before they have sufficient time to fully unwind and organize into the optimal all-trans structure. This often results in a higher fraction of random coils or less ordered phases (like the α-phase).
This phenomenon is supported by literature on PVDF-based systems (J. Appl. Polym. Sci., 2010, 116, 2, 785-791) 3, which reports that slower evaporation favors the polar β-phase. Our gradual heating process deliberately creates this evaporation rate gradient, thereby programming the gradient in chain conformation. The role of the PDs is to further promote and stabilize the all-trans conformation locally via hydrogen bonding, amplifying the final effect of this physically templated gradient.
To address the Reviewer’s suggestion,
We have clarified this mechanism in the revised manuscript (Page 5).
“The gradient distribution of the all-trans conformation, rather than the spatial distribution of PDs, is the primary outcome of our gradual-heating process. While the PDs are uniformly dispersed due to good compatibility with the terpolymer matrix, the thermal gradient during film formation creates a corresponding solvent evaporation rate gradient. The bottom surface of the film, experiencing a slower evaporation rate, facilitates a more orderly arrangement of polymer chains into the all-trans conformation. The PDs, rich in hydrogen-bonding sites, locally amplify this effect by stabilizing the all-trans conformation around them. Thus, the driving force is the evaporation rate gradient templated by the thermal gradient, which directly programs the gradient in polymer chain conformation.”
8. The article shows that the material performs best at 0.5 wt% PDs. Please explain why the material's performance declines when the PDs content exceeds 0.5 wt% and provide relevant supporting materials.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful question regarding the optimal PDs content. We have conducted a thorough analysis and propose the following mechanisms, supported by relevant literature, to explain the performance decline beyond 0.5 wt% PDs. The decline in electrostrictive strain at higher PDs loadings is likely attributable to two interrelated factors:
Increased Material Modulus and Restricted Chain Mobility: While the hydrogen bonds between PDs and the terpolymer matrix are crucial for promoting the electroactive all-trans conformation, an excessive density of these hydrogen bonds can form a rigid network that acts as physical cross-links. This network significantly restricts the mobility of the polymer chains. Since the large electrostrictive strain in relaxor ferroelectrics relies on the reorientation of polar segments under an electric field, this increased modulus directly impedes the achievable strain.
Inhibition of Dipole Switching under Electric Field: The hydrogen bonds effectively stabilize the all-trans conformations. However, beyond an optimal concentration, these bonds may become too numerous and stable, effectively "locking" the dipoles in place. In an alternating electric field, these overly stabilized dipoles cannot switch orientation freely, leading to a decrease in polarization response and thus a lower electrostrictive strain.
In summary, we posit that at 0.5 wt% PDs, a balance is achieved where hydrogen bonds optimally promote the all-trans conformation without excessively restricting chain mobility or dipole switching. At higher loadings, the detrimental effects of increased modulus and inhibited dipole reversal outweigh the benefits of further increasing the all-trans conformation content.
To address the Reviewer’s suggestion,
We have added the following content on Page 5 of the revised manuscript.
" Figs. 1e and S1a illustrate the thickness strain (S3) of nanocomposites with different concentrations of PDs as a function of electric field. As PD content increases, the strain initially rises and then decreases, and the composite with 0.5 wt% PDs content has the highest strain. This is due to the best hydrogen bonding interactions between PDs and terpolymer in the 0.5 wt% PDs doped composites."
9. Please provide the DSC test results for pure terpolymers (terpolymer-G) and composite materials with different PDs contents (terpolymer/PDs-G).
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have conducted DSC measurements (Fig. R5). The DSC data from the second heating cycle show a clear trend: both the melting temperature and the melting enthalpy of the composite films gradually decrease as the PDs content increases. This phenomenon indicates that the incorporation of PDs influences the thermal behavior and microstructure of the polymer matrix.
We interpret these observations in the context of the all-trans conformation. The formation of hydrogen bonds between PDs and the terpolymer chains is known to promote the all-trans conformation. The changes in thermal properties observed by DSC suggest that this interaction also alters the packing and organization of the polymer chains on a broader scale. The specific nature of this microstructural evolution, as reflected in the thermal data, is a subject of our ongoing investigation.
Fig. R5 The second heating curves of the terpolymer-G and composite materials with different PDs contents.
To address the Reviewer’s suggestion,
We have supplemented the relevant discussion in the revised manuscript (Page 7). The DSC test results have been added to the revised supporting information as Fig. S3.
“The thermal properties of the composites with varying PDs contents were characterized by differential scanning calorimetric (DSC). The second heating cycle revealed that both the melting temperature and melting enthalpy of the composite films exhibited a gradual decrease with increasing PDs content (Fig. S3). Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript, "Biomimetic actuator crafted from a relaxor ferroelectric polymer nanocomposite," presents the fabrication of a single-layer actuator based on a P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) terpolymer with a gradient distribution of polymer dots (PDs). The authors claim that this novel structure leads to a functional unimorph actuator with exceptionally high strain (14.4% at 100 MV/m) and ultra-low power consumption (3-8 mW), demonstrating its potential through caterpillar-like and butterfly-like soft robots. While the concept of creating a functional gradient within a single material is intriguing and the demonstrated actuators are visually impressive, the reviewer has several major concerns regarding the experimental design, the interpretation of the results, and the validity of the central claims. These concerns are significant enough to undermine the core conclusions of the study.
In summary, the manuscript's central claims of significant material improvement, ultra-low power consumption, and practical innovation are built on a foundation of questionable baselines, inappropriate comparisons, and the omission of a critical discussion on the impracticality of the high operating voltage. While the idea is interesting, the work in its current form does not provide sufficient rigorous and contextual evidence to support its claims. Therefore, the reviewer regrets that the reviewer cannot recommend this manuscript for publication.
Response: We are truly grateful that the reviewers found our idea interesting and provided a series of constructive questions. We have carefully considered their comments and have revised the manuscript accordingly.
1. The abstract prominently features an "exceptionally high strain" of 14.4%. This is a misleading representation of the actuator's performance. The reported value is the thickness strain (S3), which is an indirect, internal material response, not the functional output of the device. For a bending actuator, the useful performance is defined by macroscopic motion, such as bending curvature, tip deflection, or angular displacement. The high thickness strain is merely the cause that, due to the engineered gradient structure, gets converted into bending. Presenting the cause as the primary performance metric in the abstract, without this critical context, conflates an intrinsic material property with a structural amplification effect. It creates the false impression that the material itself linearly contracts or expands by this magnitude, which is not the case. This is a significant overstatement of the material's direct actuation capability.
Response: Upon careful consideration, we agree that the term "thickness strain" (S3), typically used for homogeneous materials, is not the most accurate descriptor for the output of our gradient-structured films. The measured value of 14.4% ultrahigh strain in terpolymer/PDs-G films, resulting from their non-uniform deformation under an electric field, is best interpreted not as an intrinsic material property but as the actuation strain of the actuating element. This value quantifies the intense local deformation generated by the material's gradient structure, which is subsequently translated into functional, macroscopic motion of the actuator. In direct response to this comment, we have thoroughly revised our manuscript: We have revised the abstract, defining the high strain of the gradient composite film under an electric field as the actuation strain. This new phrasing directly links the high local strain to macroscopic performance. The relevant Results section now explicitly clarifies the nature of this strain measurement as the "actuation strain" that reflects the non-uniform deformation of the gradient structure.
Furthermore, we have now conducted a thorough quantification of the functional device performance. We have recorded new videos under various driving voltages and, more crucially, measured the angular displacement of our butterfly actuator as a function of the electric field (Movie R1). The new data demonstrate that the actuator's angular displacement progressively increases with the electric field, reaching nearly 90° at 50 MV m-1 (Fig. R6). This key metric of macroscopic motion directly addresses the reviewer's concern and unequivocally showcases the practical utility of our device.
We believe these revisions have eliminated any potential for misinterpretation. They more accurately frame our achievement: we developed a gradient material capable of generating an intense local driving strain, and we successfully leveraged this to achieve remarkable functional motion in actuators, quantitatively measured by their angular displacement. We thank the reviewer again for helping us articulate this with greater precision and impact.
